None of the three solutions gives a justified answer.

- **Solution 1 (50):** The "Möbius strip graph" identification is unsupported and self-contradictory. It also never checks any cut or matching.
- **Solution 2 (7):** No simple 4-regular planar graph on 7 vertices exists. The 4-regular planar graphs begin at 6 vertices (octahedron), and there are none on 7 vertices, so this answer is impossible.
- **Solution 3 (8):** It rules out the octahedron with an invalid argument. It also asserts, without verification, that the square antiprism is the unique exception.

I checked the octahedron directly. If a 1-regular conflict graph $\widehat{G}$ is a perfect matching, a conflict-free cut must avoid containing both edges of any matched pair. Every single-vertex cut forces each vertex to be the common vertex of exactly one matched pair, so the matching corresponds to an outdegree-2 orientation. A cut $S$ is blocked exactly when every vertex of $S$ has an out-neighbour in $S$ and every vertex outside $S$ has an out-neighbour outside $S$. For the octahedron, this can only happen with a pair of antipodal faces that are both directed 3-cycles. I tested the orientations forced by a source-based case analysis and found that each one contains such an antipodal pair, so they all admit a conflict-free cut. This is strong evidence that the octahedron is the exceptional graph, which would give 6 vertices. That is not among the proposed answers. This is not a full exhaustive check, since I did not finish the mixed-type orientations, so my confidence is moderate.

CHOICE: NONE
